mainTopic: Reading the מגילה before the 14th: who the early reading is for, how the days shift when פורים meets שבת, and why the מגילה is never read on שבת
overview: The amud opens by testing whether villagers read the מגילה early on the יום הכניסה to help the walled cities. Two challenges from the משנה are answered. A third, from רבי יהודה, forces a rereading: the early reading is a kindness to the villagers, given because they already supply the cities. The גמרא then explains why the משנה lists its examples by weekday, and asks whose view the משנה follows when the 14th falls on Friday. The answer is either רבי or רבי יוסי. Each of them, and each opposing תנא קמא, draws a different feature of a normal year from ״בכל שנה ושנה״, since this calendar cannot keep them all. Next the גמרא shows that רבי moves the towns to the יום הכניסה only when their own day falls on שבת, and that רב הונא's rule follows רבי. Finally it asks why the מגילה is never read on שבת. רבה says it is a גזירה against carrying, which also covers שופר and לולב. רב יוסף says the poor are waiting for their gifts, and a corrected ברייתא supports him; it continues on the next amud.

steps.title: If the rule helps the cities, why don't villagers read early when פורים falls on Monday?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether the early reading is really a תקנה for the cities. It challenges this from the משנה's case where the fourteenth falls on Monday.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does this mean the rule was made for the benefit of the walled cities? But we learned in the משנה: if the fourteenth falls on Monday, villages and large towns read on that same day. If the rule is for the cities' benefit, the villagers should move their reading earlier, to the previous day of assembly!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the idea that villagers read early in order to help the cities. It points to a case in the משנה where the villagers do NOT read early.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Suppose the goal is to keep the villagers free on פורים to bring supplies to the cities. Then they should always read early, even when the fourteenth is on Monday, by moving back to the previous Thursday. Yet the משנה says that when the fourteenth is on Monday they read on the fourteenth itself. That seems to contradict the 'for the cities' explanation.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that to say? (introduces a doubtful conclusion)
An enactment or ordinance (תקנה) made by the Sages
But didn't we learn in a משנה? (introduces a challenge)
Day of assembly: Monday or Thursday, when villagers come into town
And if it is so (if your claim were true)

steps.confusionAlert: Watch the word 'early.' Monday the fourteenth is ITSELF a day of assembly, so the villagers read on the real date. The question is why they don't go even further back, to the previous Thursday.

phrases.english: Is that to say that the ordinance is for the benefit of the cities?
But didn't we learn in the Mishnah:
If the fourteenth fell on Monday,
villages and large towns
read on that very day.
And if it is so (that it is for the cities),
let them advance to the (previous) day of assembly!
phrases.notes: That would be the previous Thursday.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reason given on the previous amud: 'so that they supply water and food to the cities.'
steps.kashyaTarget: The assumption that the early reading is a תקנה for the benefit of the כרכין
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the goal were to free the villagers for פורים, they would always read early. But on a Monday fourteenth they read on time.

steps.title: Moving back would land on the tenth, which was never allowed
steps.stepSummary: The previous Thursday would be the tenth of אדר. The חכמים never set the tenth as a valid reading day.
steps.simpleTranslation: For them it would be the tenth, and the Sages did not establish the tenth.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. Reading early on a Monday fourteenth would mean reading on the tenth, which is outside the allowed range.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The allowed days for reading are the eleventh through the fifteenth. The Thursday before a Monday fourteenth is the tenth. The villagers cannot move back that far, so they read on the fourteenth. This has nothing to do with whom the תקנה benefits.

phrases.english: It would be, for them, the tenth,
and the Sages did not establish the tenth.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the Monday challenge.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Outside limit: the required date falls outside the permitted range of days
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The Monday case seemed to prove the תקנה is not for the cities.
steps.terutzMaskana: The villagers would read early if they could, but the tenth is not an allowed day.

steps.title: Then why don't villagers read early when פורים falls on Thursday?
steps.stepSummary: A second challenge from the משנה. When the fourteenth is on Thursday, the previous Monday is the eleventh, which IS allowed. Yet the villagers read on the fourteenth.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: if the fourteenth falls on Thursday, villages and large towns read on that same day. If the rule is for the cities' benefit, they should move back to the previous day of assembly, which is the eleventh!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new challenge. This time the 'tenth' answer cannot work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the fourteenth is on Thursday, the previous Monday is the eleventh, a valid day. If freeing the villagers for פורים were the goal, they should read on that Monday. The משנה has them read on the fourteenth instead.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear (introduces a source to prove or challenge)
The eleventh (of אדר), the earliest valid day

phrases.english: Come and hear:
If the fourteenth fell on Thursday,
villages and large towns
read on that very day.
And if it is so,
let them advance to the (previous) day of assembly,
since it is the eleventh!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new challenge that gets around the answer in step 2.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Moving back to the eleventh is allowed. If the goal were to free the villagers, they should read on that Monday.

steps.title: We don't push from one day of assembly back to another
steps.stepSummary: Thursday the fourteenth is already a day of assembly. We do not move the reading from one assembly day to an earlier one.
steps.simpleTranslation: From a day of assembly to a day of assembly we do not push off.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that when the real date is already a market day, the villagers have no reason to shift to an earlier market day.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The early-reading rule only moves villagers to the market day closest to the fourteenth. When the fourteenth is itself a market day, they read on it. Skipping back to an earlier market day is not done.

keyTerms.meaning: We do not push off or defer

phrases.english: From one day of assembly to another day of assembly
we do not defer.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִיּוֹם הַכְּנִיסָה לְיוֹם הַכְּנִיסָה לָא דָּחֵינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the Thursday challenge.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting principle on how far the reading may be moved
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any valid earlier day should be used if the goal is to help the cities.
steps.terutzMaskana: The reading is never moved from one assembly day back to an earlier assembly day.

steps.title: רבי יהודה: villagers who don't come to town read on the fourteenth
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה says early reading applies only where villagers come into town on Monday and Thursday. If the rule were for the cities, why should the cities lose out where villagers don't come in?
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: רבי יהודה said, when does this apply? In a place where people come into town on Monday and Thursday. But in a place where they do not come in on Monday and Thursday, they read it only at its proper time. Now, if you think the rule is for the benefit of the cities, should the cities lose out just because the villagers don't come in on Monday and Thursday?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a third and stronger challenge, from רבי יהודה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the goal were to free the villagers to supply the cities on פורים, the cities would need that help even where villagers don't usually come to town. Yet רבי יהודה makes the villagers there read on the fourteenth. That ties the rule to the villagers' own trips, not to the cities' needs.

keyTerms.meaning: And if it enters your mind (if you were to think)
They cause a loss, or lose out

phrases.english: Come and hear: Rabbi Yehuda said:
When (does this apply)?
In a place where they come in on Monday and Thursday.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל מְקוֹם שֶׁאֵין נִכְנָסִים בַּשֵּׁנִי וּבַחֲמִישִׁי —
phrases.english: But a place where they do not come in on Monday and Thursday,
they read it only at its proper time.
And if it enters your mind
that it is an ordinance for the cities,
because they do not come in on Monday and Thursday,
should the cities lose out?

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע, אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוּדָה: אֵימָתַי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third challenge to the same assumption. This one cannot be answered.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The cities' need does not depend on whether villagers usually come to town. So limiting the rule to villagers who come to town shows the rule serves the villagers.

steps.title: Rereading the reason: early reading is a kindness to the villagers
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא accepts the challenge and rewords the reason. It is not 'so that they can supply the cities' but 'because they already supply the cities.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Do not say 'so that they can supply water and food.' Rather say: 'because they supply water and food to their brothers in the cities.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives up the 'for the cities' reading. It changes one word in the reason so that the rule is a favor to the villagers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'So that they can supply' made the rule serve the cities. 'Because they supply' makes it a reward to the villagers, who already come to town on market days. Since they are in town anyway, they hear the מגילה then and are spared an extra trip. Where villagers don't come to town, the rule gives them nothing, so they read on the fourteenth.

keyTerms.meaning: Don't say… rather say (a rereading of a phrase)

steps.whatToRemember: The early reading on the יום הכניסה is a kindness to the villagers, because they supply the cities and come to town on market days anyway. It is not meant to free them for the cities' benefit on פורים. That is why רבי יהודה limits it to places where villagers actually come to town.
steps.confusionAlert: The two wordings look almost the same. 'כדי ש' (so that) points to a future purpose: helping the cities. 'מפני ש' (because) points to an existing reason: rewarding the villagers. The whole סוגיא turns on this difference.
steps.whyThisMatters: It explains why early reading applies only where villagers really come to town. It also explains why the הלכה ties the reading to the market days.

phrases.english: Do not say
'so that they can supply water and food,'
rather say:
'because they supply water and food
to their brothers in the cities.'

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא תֵּימָא כְּדֵי שֶׁיְּסַפְּקוּ מַיִם וּמָזוֹן, אֶלָּא אֵימָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the challenge from רבי יהודה and rewrites the earlier reason.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The תקנה of reading on the יום הכניסה is for the villagers' benefit, given because they supply the cities, so they need not make an extra trip to hear the מגילה.

steps.title: Why does the משנה switch from dates to weekdays?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's example of פורים falling on Monday. It asks why the first part of the משנה counts by dates of the month while the later part counts by days of the week.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'How so? If it falls on Monday, villages and large towns read on that day, etc.' What is different about the first part, which uses the order of the month's dates, and the later part, which uses the order of the weekdays?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic. It quotes a new line of the משנה and asks a question about its wording.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה first said the מגילה can be read on the 11th, 12th, 13th, 14th or 15th, which is a list of dates. Then it switches to examples by weekday: 'if it falls on Monday...'. The גמרא wants to know why the משנה changed its style.

keyTerms.meaning: The first clause of a משנה
The latter clause of a משנה
The order of the dates of the month
The order of the days of the week

phrases.english: How so?
If [the fourteenth] falls on Monday,

phrases.aramaic: כְּפָרִים וַעֲיָירוֹת גְּדוֹלוֹת קוֹרִין בּוֹ בַיּוֹם וְכוּ׳.
phrases.english: villages and large towns read on that day, etc.
What is different about the first clause
that it uses the order of the month (dates),
and what is different about the latter clause
that it uses the order of the days (of the week)?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי שְׁנָא רֵישָׁא דְּנָקֵט סִידּוּרָא דְיַרְחָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the topic of why villages read early and opens a new question about the style of the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the משנה lists by dates in the רישא but by weekdays in the סיפא.

steps.title: Listing by dates would scramble the weekdays
steps.stepSummary: Listing the examples by date would have put the weekdays out of order, so the משנה lists them by weekday instead.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since [the days] would be turned around for it, it used the order of the weekdays.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the wording question. Ordering the examples by date would have mixed up the weekdays.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the משנה arranged the cases by the date the villages read (11th, 12th, 13th, 14th), the weekdays would jump around. First would come a fourteenth on Sunday (read on the 11th). Next would be a fourteenth on Wednesday or שבת (read on the 12th), then a fourteenth on Tuesday or Friday (read on the 13th), and only then a fourteenth on Monday or Thursday (read on the 14th). That would be confusing to learn, so for the examples the משנה simply goes through the week in order.

keyTerms.meaning: They would be reversed or turned around
Took or used (a style of listing)

phrases.english: Since [the days] would be reversed for it,
it used the order of the days (of the week).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 7.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Listing by dates would have jumbled the weekdays, so the משנה listed the examples by weekday for clarity.
steps.whatToRemember: The משנה switches to weekdays only to keep the examples clear. It is about style, not a change in the law.

steps.title: Whose opinion is the משנה about Friday?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's case of פורים falling on Friday and asks which תנא it follows.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'If it falls on ערב שבת, etc.' Whose opinion is our משנה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next line of the משנה. It asks which תנא wrote this ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, when the 14th is Friday, only the villages read early, on Thursday. The large towns and walled cities read on Friday. The גמרא wants to identify the תנא who holds this.

phrases.english: If [the fourteenth] falls on Shabbat eve (Friday), etc.
Whose [opinion] is our mishna?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic on the next line of the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which תנא holds that on a Friday Purim only the villages move earlier.

steps.title: Either רבי or רבי יוסי
steps.stepSummary: The משנה could follow either רבי or רבי יוסי.
steps.simpleTranslation: Either רבי or רבי יוסי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with two possible authors. Next it will explain each one's view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two תנאים each give a ruling that fits the משנה. The גמרא names both now and will show the source for each.

keyTerms.meaning: רבי יהודה הנשיא, editor of the משנה
A תנא whose view is explained later

phrases.english: Either Rabbi or Rabbi Yosei.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 9.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The משנה follows either רבי or רבי יוסי.

steps.title: A ברייתא shows רבי's view
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא shows that רבי disagrees with the תנא קמא and holds that large towns are not moved earlier. This matches the משנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is רבי's view? As it was taught: if it falls on Friday, villages and large towns move earlier to the day of assembly, and walled cities read on the day itself. רבי says: I say the towns should not be pushed from their place. Rather, both these and those read on the day itself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the first option, רבי. It quotes a ברייתא where רבי's ruling matches the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תנא קמא in the ברייתא has the large towns read early on Thursday along with the villages. רבי says the towns stay on their normal day, the 14th, together with the walled cities. That is exactly what the משנה says, so the משנה can be רבי.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is taught (in a ברייתא)
They should not be pushed off

steps.confusionAlert: Here רבי means רבי יהודה הנשיא. He is a different תנא from רבי יהודה quoted in step 5.

phrases.english: What is [the view of] Rabbi?
As it is taught [in a baraita]:
If [the fourteenth] falls on Shabbat eve,
villages and large towns
advance [their reading] to the day of assembly (Thursday),
and walled cities read on that day (Friday).
Rabbi says: I say,
the towns should not be pushed from their place (their usual date),

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אֵלּוּ וָאֵלּוּ קוֹרִין בּוֹ בַיּוֹם.
phrases.english: rather, both these and those read on that day.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the first option, רבי, from step 10.
steps.raayaObject: That the משנה can follow רבי.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא where רבי rules that large towns read on Friday with the walled cities, unlike the תנא קמא.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that a Friday Purim was debated. The משנה's ruling that the towns read on the day itself fits רבי's side of the debate.

steps.title: What is the reason of the first opinion?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the source behind the תנא קמא's view that large towns move earlier to Thursday.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason of the first תנא?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the תנא קמא in the ברייתא holds that large towns move their reading earlier. This question sets up the explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 11 showed that רבי disagrees with the תנא קמא. Now the גמרא wants to know what each side is based on, starting with the תנא קמא.

keyTerms.meaning: The first, unnamed opinion in a משנה or ברייתא

phrases.english: What is the reason of the first tanna?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After establishing the dispute between the תנא קמא and רבי, the גמרא asks for the source of the תנא קמא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The scriptural or logical basis for moving the large towns earlier.

steps.title: Towns must always come before walled cities
steps.stepSummary: The תנא קמא learns from "בכל שנה ושנה" that, as every year, the towns must read one day before the walled cities.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because it is written: "in every year." Just as every year the towns come before the walled cities, so too here the towns come before the walled cities.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the פסוק "בכל שנה ושנה" means Purim should look the same every year. Since towns always read a day before walled cities, they must do so this year too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This year the walled cities move back from שבת to Friday, the 14th. To stay one day ahead of them, the towns must move to Thursday, the 13th. The תנא קמא treats the order (towns first) as the feature that must be kept.

keyTerms.meaning: Large towns without walls, which normally read on the 14th
Walled cities, which normally read on the 15th

phrases.english: As it is written: "in every year."
Just as every year
the towns come before the walled cities,
so too here the towns come before the walled cities.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about the reason of the תנא קמא.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק "בכל שנה ושנה" requires keeping the yearly order in which towns read before walled cities.

steps.title: Maybe the verse means towns stay on their usual date
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: "בכל שנה ושנה" could just as well mean the towns keep their usual date, the 14th.
steps.simpleTranslation: But say instead: "in every year" means that just as every year the towns are not pushed from their date, so too here the towns should not be pushed from their date!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the תנא קמא. The same פסוק could point to a different feature of every year: the towns always read on the 14th.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every normal year has two features: towns read first, and towns read on the 14th. The challenge asks why the תנא קמא keeps the order and gives up the date, when the פסוק could be read the other way.

keyTerms.meaning: "But say instead". It introduces an alternate reading that challenges the first one.
From their usual place, here meaning their usual date

phrases.english: But say: "in every year,"
just as every year
the towns are not pushed from their usual date,

phrases.aramaic: אַף כָּאן לֹא יִדָּחוּ עֲיָירוֹת מִמְּקוֹמָן!
phrases.english: so too here the towns should not be pushed from their usual date!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the תנא קמא's reading of the פסוק by offering an alternative reading.
steps.kashyaTarget: The תנא קמא's use of "בכל שנה ושנה" to require that towns come first
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same פסוק could support keeping the usual date (the 14th) instead of the usual order.

steps.title: Here both cannot be kept
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that this case is different because both features of a normal year cannot be kept at once.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here it is different, because it is impossible.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends the תנא קמא. This year the towns cannot both read on the 14th and read before the walled cities, so one feature has to give way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תירוץ does not prove that the order matters more. It only explains that a choice is forced, and the תנא קמא chose to keep the order. The alternate reading in step 14 is therefore not a refutation, just the other possible choice.
steps.confusionAlert: This answer does not say the 14th is unimportant. It says that both the 14th and "towns first" cannot be kept this year, so the תנא קמא keeps one of them.

phrases.english: Here it is different, for it is not possible.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא against the תנא קמא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Forced choice: both conditions cannot be fulfilled, so one must yield.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק equally implies keeping the date, so the תנא קמא's reading seems arbitrary.
steps.terutzMaskana: Because both cannot be kept, the תנא קמא may choose to keep the order of towns before walled cities.

steps.title: What is רבי's reason?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא now asks for רבי's source for keeping the towns on the 14th.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי, what is his reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to the other side of the dispute and asks why רבי holds that the towns are not moved. This sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now that the תנא קמא's source is explained, the גמרא does the same for רבי, who ruled in step 11 that the towns stay in place.

keyTerms.meaning: רבי יהודה הנשיא, the compiler of the משנה

phrases.english: And Rabbi, what is his reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the תנא קמא's reason to רבי's reason.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The basis for רבי's view that the large towns are not moved from the 14th.

steps.title: Towns always keep their date
steps.stepSummary: רבי learns from the same פסוק that, as every year, the towns stay on the 14th.
steps.simpleTranslation: "In every year": just as every year the towns are not pushed from their date, so too here the towns are not pushed from their date.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבי uses the same פסוק but keeps the other feature: the towns always read on the 14th.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי's reading is exactly the alternate reading that challenged the תנא קמא in step 14. For רבי, the fixed date is what must stay the same every year, even though this means the towns and walled cities read on the same day.

keyTerms.meaning: They will be pushed away or moved

phrases.english: "In every year":
just as every year
the towns are not pushed from their usual date,

phrases.aramaic: אַף כָּאן לֹא יִדָּחוּ עֲיָירוֹת מִמְּקוֹמָן.
phrases.english: so too here the towns are not pushed from their usual date.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּכׇל שָׁנָה וְשָׁנָה, מָה כׇּל שָׁנָה וְשָׁנָה אֵין עֲיָירוֹת נִדְחִין מִמְּקוֹמָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about רבי's reason.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: "בכל שנה ושנה" requires keeping the towns' fixed date of the 14th.

steps.title: Maybe the verse means towns must come first
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי with the תנא קמא's reading: the פסוק could mean towns must always come first.
steps.simpleTranslation: But say instead: "in every year" means that just as every year the towns come before the walled cities, so too here the towns should come before the walled cities!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי the same way it challenged the תנא קמא. The פסוק could mean the towns must keep their place before the walled cities.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the mirror image of step 14. The reading that the תנא קמא used now serves as the challenge to רבי.

keyTerms.meaning: "Just as ... so too". It is the pattern used to compare one case to another.

phrases.english: But say: "in every year,"
just as every year
the towns come before the walled cities,

phrases.aramaic: אַף כָּאן נָמֵי עֲיָירוֹת קוֹדְמוֹת לַמּוּקָּפִין!
phrases.english: so too here also the towns should come before the walled cities!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי's reading by offering the תנא קמא's reading of the same פסוק.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי's use of "בכל שנה ושנה" to keep the towns on the 14th
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same פסוק could support keeping the usual order (towns first) instead of the usual date.

steps.title: Here too both cannot be kept
steps.stepSummary: The same answer defends רבי: both features cannot be kept, so רבי chooses to keep the date.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here it is different, because it is impossible.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רבי with the same answer it gave for the תנא קמא. Since both features cannot be kept, רבי may choose to keep the 14th.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This exchange between the תנא קמא and רבי ends balanced. Both sides use the same פסוק, but each draws a different feature of a normal year from it, and each side's reading is simply the challenge against the other side. The real disagreement is which feature matters more: the order or the date. The גמרא now goes on to explain רבי יוסי's view in the same way.

keyTerms.meaning: The 14th of אדר, the towns' normal reading day
The 13th of אדר, the day the תנא קמא moves the towns to in this case
Friday, the day the walled cities read when the 15th falls on שבת

steps.whatToRemember: Both the תנא קמא and רבי learn from "בכל שנה ושנה" that this year should look like every year. Because both features cannot be kept, the תנא קמא keeps the order (towns first, so they read on Thursday), and רבי keeps the date (towns stay on Friday, the 14th).
steps.whyThisMatters: This explains how the משנה's case of Purim on Friday fits רבי. The towns stay on the 14th and read together with the walled cities.

phrases.english: Here it is different, for it is not possible.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא against רבי, mirroring step 15.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Forced choice: both conditions cannot be fulfilled, so one must yield.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק equally implies keeping the order, so רבי's reading seems arbitrary.
steps.terutzMaskana: Because both cannot be kept, רבי may choose to keep the towns' fixed date of the 14th.

steps.title: What is רבי יוסי's view?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what exactly the opinion of רבי יוסי is.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the opinion of רבי יוסי?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what רבי יוסי's opinion is. This is a setup line, and the answer comes in the next step from a ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוסי's name has come up in the discussion, but his actual ruling has not yet been spelled out. Before comparing his view to the others, the גמרא needs to state it clearly.

keyTerms.meaning: A תנא whose view is quoted in the ברייתא

phrases.english: What is [the view of] Rabbi Yosei?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Having finished רבי's view, the גמרא explains the second option from step 10: that the משנה may follow רבי יוסי.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The content of רבי יוסי's ruling.

steps.title: The ברייתא: walled cities move earlier, or read with the towns
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא records a dispute for when the 14th falls on Friday. The תנא קמא moves walled cities and villages to Thursday. רבי יוסי says walled cities never read before towns, so both read on Friday.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught in a ברייתא: If the 14th falls on Friday, the walled cities and the villages move their reading earlier, to the day of assembly. The large towns read on the day itself. רבי יוסי says: walled cities do not go before the towns. Rather, both of them read on that day.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a ברייתא that shows a dispute about the year when the 14th of Adar is on Friday.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Walled cities normally read on the 15th, but here the 15th is שבת. The תנא קמא sends them back to Thursday, which puts them a day before the towns. רבי יוסי refuses to let walled cities go before towns, so he has them read on Friday together with the towns.

keyTerms.meaning: As it was taught in a ברייתא
Walled cities, which normally read on the 15th
The day of assembly (Monday or Thursday), when villagers came to town
Large towns, which normally read on the 14th

steps.confusionAlert: ״בו ביום״ in רבי יוסי's statement means Friday, the 14th. It does not mean the walled cities' own day, which is the 15th.

phrases.english: As it is taught: If it occurs on Shabbat eve,
walled cities and villages move earlier to the day of assembly,
and large towns read on the day itself.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יוֹסֵי אוֹמֵר: אֵין מוּקָּפִין קוֹדְמִין לַעֲיָירוֹת,
phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei says: walled cities do not precede towns,

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אֵלּוּ וָאֵלּוּ קוֹרִין בּוֹ בַיּוֹם.
phrases.english: rather, both these and those read on that day.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 20 by quoting the ברייתא.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי יוסי holds that walled cities never read before towns, so when the 14th is Friday both read on Friday.

steps.title: What is the תנא קמא's source?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reasoning of the תנא קמא.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason of the תנא קמא?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the תנא קמא moves the walled cities to Thursday. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Moving the walled cities to Thursday puts them before the towns, which is unusual. The גמרא wants to know what source supports this.

keyTerms.meaning: The first, unnamed opinion in a ברייתא or משנה

phrases.english: What is the reason of the first tanna?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source behind the first opinion in the ברייתא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The scriptural basis for moving walled cities to Thursday.

steps.title: As every year: towns on the 14th, and the two never share a day
steps.stepSummary: The תנא קמא learns from ״בכל שנה ושנה״ that this year should look like every year. Towns read on the 14th, and towns and walled cities read on different days.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written, ״בכל שנה ושנה״, "in every year." Just as every year the towns read on the 14th, and the time of one is not the time of the other, so too here the towns read on the 14th, and the time of one is not the time of the other.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that the תנא קמא copies two features of a normal year into this year.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first feature is that towns read on the 14th, so they stay on Friday. The second is that towns and walled cities never read on the same day. Since the walled cities cannot read on Friday and cannot read on שבת, they must go back to Thursday.

keyTerms.term: זְמַנּוֹ שֶׁל זֶה לֹא זְמַנּוֹ שֶׁל זֶה
keyTerms.meaning: The time of one is not the time of the other

phrases.english: As it is written: "In every year,"

phrases.aramaic: מָה כׇּל שָׁנָה וְשָׁנָה עֲיָירוֹת בְּאַרְבָּעָה עָשָׂר,
phrases.english: just as every year the towns are on the fourteenth,

phrases.aramaic: וּזְמַנּוֹ שֶׁל זֶה לֹא זְמַנּוֹ שֶׁל זֶה —
phrases.english: and the time of this one is not the time of that one,
so too here, the towns are on the fourteenth,

phrases.aramaic: וּזְמַנּוֹ שֶׁל זֶה לֹא זְמַנּוֹ שֶׁל זֶה.
phrases.english: and the time of this one is not the time of that one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 22.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: ״בכל שנה ושנה״ keeps two features: towns on the 14th, and separate days for towns and walled cities.

steps.title: Challenge: every year walled cities never come first
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the תנא קמא. The same פסוק could teach a different feature of a normal year: walled cities never read before towns.
steps.simpleTranslation: But say instead: ״בכל שנה ושנה״. Just as every year the walled cities do not go before the towns, so too here the walled cities should not go before the towns!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the תנא קמא using his own פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תנא קמא's ruling puts the walled cities on Thursday, before the towns. That breaks a third feature of every normal year: walled cities always read after towns. So the same פסוק seems to argue against him.

phrases.english: But say: "In every year,"
just as every year
walled cities do not precede the towns,

phrases.aramaic: אַף כָּאן אֵין מוּקָּפִין קוֹדְמִין לָעֲיָירוֹת!
phrases.english: so too here, walled cities should not precede the towns!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the derivation in step 23.
steps.kashyaTarget: The תנא קמא's ruling that walled cities move to Thursday.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק that copies the normal year should also copy the rule that walled cities never come before towns, and the תנא קמא breaks that rule.

steps.title: Here it is impossible to keep everything
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that this case is different, because not every feature of a normal year can be kept at once.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is different here, because it is not possible.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends the תנא קמא: in this case something has to give.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Three features cannot all be kept: towns on the 14th, separate days, and walled cities never first. The תנא קמא chooses to keep the first two, so he gives up the third. This is the same answer the גמרא gave for the first ברייתא's תנא קמא in step 15 and for רבי in step 19.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows how the whole סוגיא works. Each opinion keeps some features of a normal year, and the dispute is only about which feature to give up.

phrases.english: Here it is different, since it is not possible.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 24.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Practical impossibility forces a choice among conflicting derived features.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק requires every feature of a normal year, including that walled cities never come first.
steps.terutzMaskana: Not every feature can be kept here, so the תנא קמא keeps 'towns on the 14th' and 'separate days.'

steps.title: What is רבי יוסי's source?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for רבי יוסי's reasoning.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason of רבי יוסי?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now asks for the source of רבי יוסי's ruling. This sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now that the תנא קמא's reasoning is explained, the גמרא turns to the other side of the dispute.

phrases.english: What is the reason of Rabbi Yosei?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from the תנא קמא to the second opinion in the ברייתא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The scriptural basis for having walled cities read on Friday with the towns.

steps.title: As every year: walled cities never come first
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי reads ״בכל שנה ושנה״ as keeping the rule that walled cities never read before towns.
steps.simpleTranslation: ״בכל שנה ושנה״. Just as every year the walled cities do not go before the towns, so too here the walled cities do not go before the towns.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that רבי יוסי uses the same פסוק but keeps a different feature of the normal year.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוסי keeps the rule that walled cities never come first, so he will not move them to Thursday. The cost is that towns and walled cities read on the same day, Friday. Both sides agree with the reasoning of step 25 and only disagree about which feature to give up.
steps.whatToRemember: When the 14th falls on Friday, both sides learn from ״בכל שנה ושנה״. The תנא קמא keeps 'separate days,' so walled cities move to Thursday. רבי יוסי keeps 'walled cities never first,' so both read on Friday.

phrases.english: "In every year,"
just as every year
walled cities do not precede the towns,

phrases.aramaic: אַף כָּאן אֵין מוּקָּפִין קוֹדְמִין לָעֲיָירוֹת.
phrases.english: so too here, walled cities do not precede the towns.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּכׇל שָׁנָה וְשָׁנָה, מָה כׇּל שָׁנָה וְשָׁנָה אֵין מוּקָּפִין קוֹדְמִין לָעֲיָירוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 26 by repeating the reading that was raised as a challenge in step 24, now as רבי יוסי's actual source.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: ״בכל שנה ושנה״ keeps the rule that walled cities never read before towns, so both read on Friday.

steps.title: Challenging רבי יוסי with the other reading of the same verse
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא turns the earlier question around and asks רבי יוסי why ״בכל שנה ושנה״ should not mean that towns and walled cities must read on different days.
steps.simpleTranslation: But say that ״in every year״ means this: just as every year the time of one group is not the time of the other, so too here the time of one group should not be the time of the other.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now challenges רבי יוסי the same way it challenged the תנא קמא. The same verse could teach the other feature of a normal year: towns and walled cities never read on the same day.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוסי took ״בכל שנה ושנה״ to mean that walled cities never read before towns. But in a normal year the two groups also read on different days. So why not use the verse to keep that feature instead, and have the walled cities read on a separate day?

keyTerms.meaning: But say instead (introduces another possible reading)
The time of this one (this group's reading day)

phrases.english: But say: "in every year"
just as in every year

phrases.aramaic: זְמַנּוֹ שֶׁל זֶה לֹא זְמַנּוֹ שֶׁל זֶה
phrases.english: the time of this one is not the time of that one
phrases.notes: In a normal year towns read on the 14th and walled cities on the 15th.

phrases.aramaic: אַף כָּאן זְמַנּוֹ שֶׁל זֶה לֹא זְמַנּוֹ שֶׁל זֶה!
phrases.english: so too here, the time of this one should not be the time of that one!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the reading רבי יוסי gave in Step 27. It mirrors the challenge made against the תנא קמא in Step 24.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוסי's reading of ״בכל שנה ושנה״
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The verse could just as easily teach that the two groups read on different days, which is the feature רבי יוסי gives up.

steps.title: It is impossible to keep every feature of a normal year
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that this year is different. Not every feature of a normal year can be kept, so רבי יוסי chooses one of them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here it is different, because it is not possible.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רבי יוסי with the same answer it gave for the תנא קמא. This year we cannot keep every pattern at once.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This year's calendar forces a choice between two features of a normal year. Both opinions agree that only one can be kept. They just disagree about which one the verse protects.
steps.whatToRemember: The תנא קמא and רבי יוסי both use ״בכל שנה ושנה״. Since this year's calendar cannot match a normal year in every way, each one picks a different feature to keep.

phrases.english: Here it is different, because it is not possible.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 28 the same way Step 25 answered Step 24.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Impossibility: not every feature of a normal year can be kept at once.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The verse should force every feature of a normal year, including separate days.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only one feature can be kept, and רבי יוסי reasonably chooses that walled cities never read before towns.

steps.title: Does רבי really never push the towns to יום הכניסה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי's view that towns are not moved to יום הכניסה. It cites a ברייתא where רבי himself moves the towns to יום הכניסה when פורים falls on שבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does רבי hold that we do not push the towns to the day of gathering? But a ברייתא teaches: if the 14th falls on שבת, villages move their reading earlier to the day of gathering, large towns read on Friday, and walled cities read the next day. רבי says: I say that since the towns were already pushed from their proper day, let them be pushed all the way to the day of gathering.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now checks רבי for consistency. In the Friday case he keeps the towns on their own day, but this ברייתא shows him moving the towns to יום הכניסה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the 14th is on Friday, רבי has the towns read on Friday and not on Thursday. Yet when the 14th is on שבת, he moves the towns all the way back to Thursday, which is יום הכניסה. That looks like a contradiction: he seems willing to push towns to יום הכניסה after all.

keyTerms.meaning: The day of gathering (Monday or Thursday, when villagers came to town)
Cities walled since the days of יהושע
But isn't it taught in a ברייתא?
Since they were already pushed off

steps.confusionAlert: ״רבי״ with no name after it always means רבי יהודה הנשיא, who compiled the משנה. It does not mean "some rabbi."

phrases.aramaic: וְסָבַר רַבִּי עֲיָירוֹת לָא דָּחִינַן לְיוֹם הַכְּנִיסָה?
phrases.english: And does Rabbi hold that we do not push the towns to the day of gathering?
But isn't it taught: if the fourteenth falls on Shabbat
villages move earlier to the day of gathering
and large towns read on Shabbat eve (Friday)
and walled cities read the next day (Sunday, the 15th)
Rabbi says: I say
since the towns were already pushed from their proper day
let them be pushed to the day of gathering (Thursday).

steps.triggerLanguage: וְסָבַר רַבִּי עֲיָירוֹת לָא דָּחִינַן לְיוֹם הַכְּנִיסָה? וְהָתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from רבי יוסי to רבי. It tests whether רבי's ruling in the Friday case fits with another ruling of his.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי's view that towns are not pushed to יום הכניסה when the 14th is on Friday
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא shows רבי pushing towns to יום הכניסה when the 14th falls on שבת. So why not also in the Friday case?

steps.title: On שבת the towns lost their day; on Friday they did not
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that the cases are different. When the 14th is on שבת, the towns' own day cannot be used, so once they are moved anyway they can go to יום הכניסה. When the 14th is on Friday, the towns' own day is perfectly usable.
steps.simpleTranslation: How can you compare? There, their proper day is שבת, so since they are being pushed anyway, they get pushed to the day of gathering. But here, their proper day is Friday!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by showing a key difference between the two cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The reasoning ״הואיל ונדחו״ only works when the towns already lost their own day. On שבת we do not read the מגילה, so the towns must move anyway, and רבי moves them to יום הכניסה. On Friday nothing forces them to move, so they read on their own day.

keyTerms.meaning: How can these compare? (rejecting a comparison)

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that ״הואיל ונדחו״ has a limit. A group is only moved further if it has already been pushed off its own day.

phrases.english: How can these be compared?
There, their proper time is Shabbat
and since they were pushed off, let them be pushed (to the day of gathering).
But here, their proper time is Shabbat eve (Friday)!

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכִי הַשְׁתָּא? הָתָם זְמַנָּם שַׁבָּת הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in Step 30 by showing that the two cases differ.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases: in one case the towns lost their own day, in the other they did not.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי pushes towns to יום הכניסה in every case.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי pushes towns to יום הכניסה only when their own day (the 14th) falls on שבת and cannot be used.

steps.title: Whose view does רב הונא's rule follow?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes רב הונא's rule that when פורים falls on שבת everyone is pushed to יום הכניסה, and asks which תנא it follows.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whose view does this follow, which רבי חלבו said in the name of רב הונא: when פורים falls on שבת, everyone is pushed to the day of gathering?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a later rule and asks which opinion it matches. This sets up the next moves: first the wording of the rule is fixed, then the answer comes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב הונא's rule seems connected to the ברייתא just quoted. Before saying whose view it follows, the גמרא will first notice a problem with how the rule is worded.

keyTerms.meaning: According to whom does this go?
An אמורא who transmits רב הונא's teaching

phrases.english: According to whom does this go

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַבִּי חֶלְבּוֹ אָמַר רַב הוּנָא:
phrases.english: that Rabbi Chelbo said in the name of Rav Huna:
Purim that falls on Shabbat
everyone is pushed to the day of gathering.

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּמַאן אָזְלָא הָא דְּאָמַר רַבִּי חֶלְבּוֹ אָמַר רַב הוּנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the ברייתא from Step 30 by asking which opinion an אמורא's rule matches.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which תנא's view does רב הונא's rule follow?

steps.title: Not everyone can be pushed: walled cities read on Sunday
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects to the wording ״everyone is pushed,״ because walled cities read the next day and are not pushed at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: Could you really think that everyone is pushed? But there are walled cities that read the next day!
steps.whatsHappening: Before answering, the גמרא points out that רב הונא's words cannot be meant literally.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the 14th is on שבת, the 15th is Sunday, so walled cities simply read on their own day. Since they are never moved, the rule cannot say that ״everyone″ is pushed to יום הכניסה.

keyTerms.meaning: Could it enter your mind? (this cannot be right)

phrases.english: Could it enter your mind that everyone is pushed?!
But there are walled cities that observe it the next day!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the wording of the rule quoted in Step 32.
steps.kashyaTarget: The word ״הכל״ (everyone) in רב הונא's rule
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Walled cities read on Sunday, their own day, so not everyone is pushed.

steps.title: Corrected wording: whoever is pushed goes to יום הכניסה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rewords רב הונא's rule: anyone who must be moved is moved all the way to יום הכניסה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it means: whoever is pushed off is pushed to the day of gathering.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes the wording of רב הונא's rule so that it fits the facts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule does not include the walled cities. It means that any group whose own day was lost goes to יום הכניסה, and not just to Friday. That covers the villages and also the towns.

phrases.english: Rather: whoever is pushed off
is pushed to the day of gathering.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא: כׇּל הַנִּדְחֶה יִדָּחֶה לְיוֹם הַכְּנִיסָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the wording problem raised in Step 33.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Every group, including walled cities, is pushed to יום הכניסה.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only groups whose own day is lost are pushed, and they go to יום הכניסה.

steps.title: רב הונא follows רבי
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers its question: רב הונא's corrected rule follows רבי.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to whom? According to רבי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finally answers the question from Step 32: the rule matches רבי's opinion in the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the ברייתא, the first opinion had the towns read on Friday. Only רבי said that since the towns were pushed off, they go all the way to יום הכניסה. ״Whoever is pushed is pushed to יום הכניסה״ is exactly רבי's position.
steps.whatToRemember: When פורים falls on שבת: villages and towns both read on Thursday, which is יום הכניסה, and walled cities read on Sunday. This follows רבי and is taught by רב הונא. But when the 14th is on Friday, רבי keeps the towns on Friday, because their own day was never lost.

phrases.english: According to whom? According to Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from Step 32, now that the wording was fixed in Step 34.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רב הונא's rule follows רבי, who said that towns pushed off their day go to יום הכניסה.

steps.title: Everyone agrees the מגילה is not read on שבת: why?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא draws out a point all the opinions share: no one reads the מגילה on שבת. Then it asks for the reason.
steps.simpleTranslation: In any case, according to everyone, we do not read the מגילה on שבת. What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out the one thing all the opinions agree on. Then it asks why, which sets up the answers that follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every view discussed so far moves the reading off שבת, either earlier or later. None of them reads it on שבת itself. Reading the מגילה is not מלאכה, so the גמרא needs to explain why it is avoided.

phrases.english: In any case, according to everyone,
we do not read the Megillah on Shabbat.
What is the reason?

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא מִיהָא מְגִילָּה בְּשַׁבָּת לָא קָרִינַן. מַאי טַעְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the specific disputes to the one rule they all share, and asks for its reason.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason the מגילה is not read on שבת, even though reading is not a forbidden מלאכה.

steps.title: רבה: a גזירה against carrying the מגילה to an expert
steps.stepSummary: רבה explains that the חכמים made a גזירה. Since not everyone knows how to read, someone might carry the מגילה four אמות in רשות הרבים on his way to an expert.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: Everyone is obligated to read the מגילה (and to hear the שופר), but not everyone knows how to read the מגילה. So the חכמים made a decree: perhaps a person will take it in his hand, go to an expert to learn, and carry it four אמות in רשות הרבים.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה answers the question. The rule is a protective decree, a גזירה, made so that people will not come to carry on שבת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two facts combine here. Everyone is obligated, but many people do not know how to read. Someone eager to do the מצוה might grab the scroll and walk to an expert, forgetting that carrying in רשות הרבים is forbidden on שבת. To prevent that, the חכמים cancelled the reading on שבת altogether.

keyTerms.meaning: Four cubits, the distance that makes carrying forbidden

steps.confusionAlert: Reading the מגילה is not itself forbidden on שבת. The worry is only that it could lead to carrying.

phrases.english: Rabbah said:
Everyone is obligated in reading the Megillah
(and in blowing the shofar),
and not everyone is expert in reading the Megillah.
A decree: perhaps he will take it in his hand
and go to an expert to learn,
and carry it four cubits in the public domain.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה: הַכֹּל חַיָּיבִין בִּקְרִיאַת מְגִילָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 36.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A גזירה: someone might carry the מגילה four אמות in רשות הרבים while going to an expert to learn it.
steps.whyThisMatters: This same גזירה is the well-known source for why שופר and לולב are also set aside on שבת.

steps.title: The same reason applies to שופר and לולב
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא adds that רבה's concern about carrying is also why we do not blow שופר or take לולב on שבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this is the reason for שופר, and this is the reason for לולב.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא applies רבה's reason to two other מצוות that are also set aside on שבת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שופר on ראש השנה and לולב on סוכות share the same features as the מגילה. Everyone is obligated, and not everyone knows how to do the מצוה. So the same fear of carrying to an expert applies to them.

keyTerms.meaning: The ram's horn blown on ראש השנה
The palm branch taken on סוכות

steps.whatToRemember: One גזירה about carrying explains three rules: no מגילה, no שופר, and no לולב on שבת.

phrases.english: And this is the reason for the shofar.
And this is the reason for the lulav.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Widens רבה's answer to cover other מצוות.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The concern about carrying is also why שופר is not blown and לולב is not taken on שבת.

steps.title: רב יוסף: the poor are waiting for their gifts
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף gives a different reason. The poor are waiting for the reading day to receive gifts, and gifts cannot be given out on שבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: Because the eyes of the poor are lifted toward the reading of the מגילה.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף offers a second answer to the question of why the מגילה is not read on שבת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: מתנות לאביונים, the gifts to the poor, are given on the day the מגילה is read. On שבת money cannot be collected or handed out. If the reading took place on שבת, the poor would be disappointed, so the reading is moved to a weekday.

keyTerms.meaning: Gifts to the poor given on פורים

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said:
Because the eyes of the poor
are lifted toward the reading of the Megillah.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב יוֹסֵף אָמַר: מִפְּנֵי שֶׁעֵינֵיהֶן שֶׁל עֲנִיִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second answer to the question of step 36, separate from רבה's.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The poor expect their gifts on the reading day, and gifts cannot be given on שבת.

steps.title: A ברייתא supports רב יוסף
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that villages reading early on the יום הכניסה also collect and hand out the gifts on that same day.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was also taught this way: Even though they said villages move earlier to the יום הכניסה, they collect on that day and distribute on that day.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to back up רב יוסף. It shows that the gifts for the poor are tied to the day of reading.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even when villages read early, the gifts go along with the reading day. This fits רב יוסף's idea that the poor link the reading with receiving their gifts.

keyTerms.meaning: It was also taught this way (a ברייתא supports it)

phrases.english: It was also taught so:
Even though they said
villages move earlier to the day of assembly,

phrases.aramaic: גּוֹבִין בּוֹ בַיּוֹם, וּמְחַלְּקִין בּוֹ בַיּוֹם.
phrases.english: they collect on that day and distribute on that day.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רב יוסף's reason with a ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: רב יוסף's reason that the gifts to the poor are tied to the reading day.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא: villages that read early also collect and distribute the gifts on that day.

steps.title: The word "even though" does not fit
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects to the ברייתא's wording. The gifts are given that day because the reading moved, not in spite of it.
steps.simpleTranslation: ״Even though they said״? On the contrary, it is because they said it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the wording of the ברייתא it just quoted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ״Even though״ suggests the early reading is a reason not to give gifts that day. In fact, the early reading is exactly why the gifts are given that day. So the connecting word is backwards.

phrases.english: "Even though they said"?
On the contrary, it is because they said it!

steps.triggerLanguage: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאָמְרוּ? אַדְּרַבָּה, מִשּׁוּם דְּאָמְרוּ הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the wording of the ברייתא brought as proof.
steps.kashyaTarget: The phrase ״אף על פי שאמרו״ in the ברייתא.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The early reading is the cause of giving that day, not something working against it, so ״even though״ is illogical.

steps.title: Corrected reading: "since they said"
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rewords the ברייתא to say ״since.״ Because villages read early, the gifts are given that day, since the poor are waiting for the reading. The word ״אבל״ (however) begins the next part.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, read it this way: Since they said villages move earlier to the יום הכניסה, they collect on that day and distribute on that day, because the eyes of the poor are lifted toward the reading of the מגילה. However...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes the wording of the ברייתא. Now it clearly matches רב יוסף's reason, and the ״however״ leads into the next part of the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Changing ״even though״ to ״since״ makes the early reading the cause of the early giving. The corrected text also states רב יוסף's reason word for word: the poor are waiting for the reading. The trailing ״אבל״ sets up a contrasting case on the next amud.
steps.whatToRemember: The corrected ברייתא shows that the gifts to the poor follow the day of the reading, which supports רב יוסף.

phrases.english: Rather: since they said
that villages move earlier to the day of assembly,

phrases.aramaic: גּוֹבִין בּוֹ בַיּוֹם, וּמְחַלְּקִין בּוֹ בַיּוֹם,
phrases.english: they collect on that day and distribute on that day,
because the eyes of the poor
are lifted toward the reading of the Megillah.
However,
phrases.notes: Begins the next clause of the ברייתא, which continues on the next amud.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא: הוֹאִיל וְאָמְרוּ שֶׁכְּפָרִים מַקְדִּימִין לְיוֹם הַכְּנִיסָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the wording objection by correcting the ברייתא's text.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Textual correction of the ברייתא (״since״ instead of ״even though״).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא read ״even though,״ as if the early reading worked against giving gifts that day.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא reads ״since,״ so the gifts follow the reading day because the poor are waiting for it.
